(CNN) -- Rioting has flared near Belfast on Saturday after the arrests of three men in the killings of two soldiers in Northern Ireland last week, police said. Two people in masks prepare to throw petrol bombs Saturday in Lurgan, Northern Ireland. Petrol bombs have been hurled at police in Lurgan, a town in County Armagh, 20 miles west of Belfast, police in Northern Ireland said. There are gangs of youths on the streets, authorities said, but there have been no arrests or injuries. Police announced the arrests on Saturday and said the three men have been taken to the police service's Serious Crime Suite in County Antrim. One of them, a dissident republican named Colin Duffy, is from Lurgan. They are the first arrests in connection with the March 7 shootings, which were the first fatal attack on British troops in the province for more than 12 years. The two British soldiers were shot dead at a base in Massereene, in Antrim, as they were preparing to ship out for duty in Afghanistan. The soldiers, Cengiz "Pat" Azimkar, 21, and Mark Quinsey, 23, had already packed their bags and changed into desert uniforms, authorities said. Two masked gunmen with automatic rifles shot them as the soldiers picked up a pizza delivery at the barracks, authorities said. Two other soldiers and the two pizza delivery men were seriously wounded. The shooting has sparked fears of a return to the sectarian violence that Northern Ireland suffered until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, a period known as The Troubles. A militant splinter group, the Real IRA, reportedly claimed it had carried out the attack on the soldiers. Two days after the soldiers were killed, a police officer was killed in a shooting southwest of Belfast. Constable Stephen Carroll was one of four officers who were responding to call in Craigavon when his vehicle came under fire and he was killed. Three people have been arrested in connection with the police officer's death. The Continuity IRA, a republican splinter group that does not accept the Good Friday Agreement, said it had killed Carroll, Britain's Press Association reported. Politicians from across the political spectrum have condemned the killings, with Sinn Fein deputy leader Martin McGuinness calling the killers "traitors to the island of Ireland." Sinn Fein is a predominantly Catholic party that wants Northern Ireland to leave the United Kingdom and become part of the Republic of Ireland. The party is widely thought to be linked to the Irish Republican Army. Danny Kennedy, deputy leader of the loyalist Ulster Unionist Party, which wants Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom, also condemned the attack as "wicked and murderous."

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN.com / WORLD**

### Tensions boil over in Northern Ireland as arrests in military barracks attack trigger night of violent rioting

**By Nic Robertson, CNN**  
**March 15, 2009**

**BELFAST, Northern Ireland (CNN)** -- Thick black smoke billowed over the streets of Northern Ireland overnight as violent rioting erupted across several republican strongholds, following a series of high-profile arrests connected to the deadly shooting of two British soldiers last week.

Police officers in riot gear faced a barrage of petrol bombs, bricks, and blast bombs in Lurgan, County Armagh, and parts of West Belfast, as masked youths took to the streets to protest the detention of prominent dissident republicans. 

The security forces, targeted by crowds of young men, responded with water cannons and plastic bullets in some of the worst street violence the region has seen in months.

"What we are seeing on the streets tonight is a desperate attempt by a small minority of violent dissidents to drag Northern Ireland back into the dark ages," said Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Assistant Chief Constable Area Commander Roy Toner. "They will not succeed."

### High-Profile Arrests

The flashpoint for the renewed violence was the arrest of several suspects earlier on Sunday, including high-profile republican Colin Duffy, in connection with the March 7 attack on the Massereene Army Barracks in Antrim. 

In that attack, claimed by the "Real IRA"—a violent breakaway faction of the Provisional IRA—two British soldiers, Sappers Mark Quinsey, 23, and Patrick Azimkar, 21, were shot dead as they collected a pizza delivery outside the gates of their base. They were due to deploy to Afghanistan just hours later. Two pizza delivery drivers were also critically injured.

The military attack, followed days later by the fatal shooting of PSNI Constable Stephen Carroll by another dissident group, the Continuity IRA, sent shockwaves through the region, marking the first murder of a British soldier in Northern Ireland since 1997.

### A Test for the Peace Process

For many here, the sights of burning cars and armored Land Rovers under fire evoke painful memories of "The Troubles"—the three-decade sectarian conflict that left more than 3,600 people dead before the historic Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1998.

However, political analysts point out that the political landscape today is fundamentally different.

Crucially, the political leadership of Northern Ireland’s historic republican movement has roundly condemned both the killings and the subsequent rioting. 

In an unprecedented move, Northern Ireland’s Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness—a former IRA commander—publicly labeled the dissident shooters "traitors to the island of Ireland."

"These people are intent on destroying the peace process," McGuinness told reporters in Belfast. "They are attempting to destabilize the power-sharing executive, but the political representatives of the people of Northern Ireland stand united against them."

### Fragile Calm Under Threat

Despite the condemnation from mainstream politicians, security officials acknowledge that the threat posed by dissident groups remains dangerously high.

In Lurgan, local residents reported hours of terrifying disruption as hijacked vehicles were set alight near a main railway line, forcing the suspension of train services between Belfast and Dublin.

"It was pure chaos," said one local resident, who asked not to be named out of fear of retaliation. "You had kids as young as 14 throwing petrol bombs at the police. It feels like the hatred never really left, it was just waiting under the surface."

As dawn broke on Monday, heavy rain helped clear the embers of burned-out vehicles from the streets, but security forces remain on maximum alert. 

With police holding the suspects for questioning under anti-terrorism legislation, authorities fear the fragile calm could break once again in the coming days.

***

*CNN’s Laura Smith-Spark contributed to this report.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a detailed summary of the March 2009 dissident IRA attacks in Northern Ireland, including the killings of two British soldiers, Constable Stephen Carroll, the subsequent arrests, and political reactions.
counterfactuals.output:
In March 2009, Northern Ireland experienced a severe security crisis when dissident Irish republican groups launched two separate, lethal attacks within a 48-hour period. These attacks resulted in the deaths of two British soldiers and a Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officer. 

Coming over a decade after the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, these events represented the most serious challenge to the Northern Ireland peace process in years, marking the first deaths of British military personnel in the region since 1997 and the first murder of a PSNI officer since the force’s creation in 2001.

Here is a detailed summary of the attacks, the police response, subsequent legal proceedings, and political reactions.

---

### 1. The Massereene Barracks Attack (March 7, 2009)

* **Location:** Massereene Barracks in Antrim, County Antrim.
* **Target:** Unarmed British soldiers from the 38 Engineer Regiment preparing to deploy to Afghanistan, alongside civilian delivery workers.
* **Perpetrators:** The **Real IRA (RIRA)**, a dissident republican splinter group.

#### Details of the Attack
At approximately 9:40 PM on Saturday, March 7, four British soldiers stepped outside the gates of the Massereene Barracks to receive a pizza delivery from two civilian workers. 

As they walked toward the delivery car, a green Vauxhall Cavalier pulled up outside the gates. Two masked gunmen carrying AK-47 assault rifles emerged from the vehicle and opened fire, discharging over 60 rounds. After the initial volley brought the men to the ground, the gunmen walked up to the victims and fired additional shots at point-blank range before fleeing the scene.

#### Casualties
* **Killed:** Sapper Mark Quinsey (23, from Birmingham) and Sapper Patrick Azimkar (21, from London).
* **Injured:** Two other British soldiers and the two delivery drivers (one of whom was a Polish national) were critically wounded but survived.

---

### 2. The Murder of Constable Stephen Carroll (March 9, 2009)

* **Location:** Lismore Manor housing estate in Craigavon, County Armagh.
* **Target:** Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers.
* **Perpetrators:** The **Continuity IRA (CIRA)**, another dissident republican group.

#### Details of the Attack
On the evening of Monday, March 9—less than 48 hours after the Massereene attack—police responded to a 999 call from a terrified woman whose home had been targeted by youths throwing a brick through her window. The call was a deliberate lure set up by the Continuity IRA.

As PSNI patrol cars arrived to secure the scene, a sniper positioned nearby fired a single shot using a high-powered rifle. The bullet passed through the rear window of an unmarked police car, striking 48-year-old Constable Stephen Carroll in the back of the head as he sat in the driver's seat.

#### Casualties
* **Killed:** Constable Stephen Carroll, a 24-year veteran of policing who was close to retirement. He was the first officer from the reformed PSNI (which replaced the RUC in 2001) to be killed by terrorists.

---

### 3. Police Investigations, Arrests, and Legal Proceedings

The attacks triggered massive security operations led by the PSNI, resulting in several high-profile arrests, though obtaining secure convictions proved legally complex.

#### Massereene Barracks Cases
* **Colin Duffy and Brian Shivers:** Prominent dissident republican Colin Duffy and co-accused Brian Shivers were arrested shortly after the attack. DNA evidence was found on a partially burned getaway car abandoned in County Antrim.
* **Legal Outcomes:**
  * **Brian Shivers:** Initially convicted in 2012, but his conviction was overturned on appeal in 2013 due to questionable DNA reliability. He was acquitted in a retrial in 2013.
  * **Colin Duffy:** Acquitted in January 2012. The judge ruled that while Duffy’s DNA was found on a latex glove inside the getaway car, the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that he was one of the gunmen or physically present during the shooting.
  * To date, no one remains convicted for the Massereene Barracks murders.

#### Constable Stephen Carroll Cases
* **Brendan McConville and John Paul Wootton:** Police tracked a vehicle seen near the Craigavon shooting, leading to the arrest of 38-year-old Brendan McConville and 17-year-old John Paul Wootton.
* **Legal Outcomes:**
  * In May 2012, both men were convicted of the murder of Constable Carroll. Evidence included firearms discharge residue, suspicious movements tracked by a GPS device fitted to Wootton’s car by military intelligence prior to the attack, and a coat containing McConville’s DNA.
  * In 2014, their appeals were dismissed, and they received life sentences (McConville ordered to serve a minimum of 25 years; Wootton a minimum of 18 years).

---

### 4. Political Reactions and Impact

The primary objective of the dissident groups was to undermine Northern Ireland’s power-sharing government, provoke a heavy-handed security reaction from the British state, and destabilize the peace process. However, the attacks had the opposite political effect, drawing unprecedented cross-community unity.

#### Historic Joint Response by Northern Ireland Leaders
The most significant political development was the united front presented by First Minister **Peter Robinson** (Democratic Unionist Party) and Deputy First Minister **Martin McGuinness** (Sinn Féin). 

* **McGuinness's "Traitors" Speech:** In a watershed moment for Northern Irish politics, Martin McGuinness—a former high-ranking commander in the Provisional IRA—publicly condemned the dissident attackers, calling them **"traitors to the island of Ireland."** He urged members of the nationalist/republican community to cooperate fully with the PSNI, a move that was historically unprecedented for Sinn Féin leadership.
* **Standing Together:** Robinson and McGuinness stood side-by-side with PSNI Chief Constable Sir Hugh Orde outside Stormont Castle, signaling that the power-sharing executive would not collapse or be intimidated.

#### British and Irish Government Responses
* **Gordon Brown (UK Prime Minister):** Traveled to Massereene Barracks days after the attack, stating: *"The peace process is unshakeable, and the people of Northern Ireland have made it very clear that they will not return to the past."*
* **Brian Cowen (Taoiseach / Irish Prime Minister):** Condemned the violence as a "senseless act of evil" and pledged full cooperation between the Garda Síochána (Irish police) and the PSNI to track down the killers across the border.

#### Public Reaction
Thousands of people across Northern Ireland participated in silent vigils, rallies, and lunchtime demonstrations organized by trade unions in Belfast, Derry, Craigavon, and Antrim. The broad public consensus showed overwhelming rejection of a return to paramilitary violence.

---

### Summary of Significance

The March 2009 attacks were a critical stress test for Northern Ireland’s political institutions established under the peace process. Rather than reigniting sectarian conflict or destroying power-sharing, the attacks forced mainstream political enemies—unionists and republicans—to cooperate closely, thereby solidifying the political legitimacy of the PSNI and the Northern Ireland Assembly.

McGuinness's stance is seen by analysts as a vital bulwark against a return to sectarian violence, as it signals that mainstream republicanism will not offer safe harbor to armed dissidents. 

Despite the unified political condemnation, security analysts warn that the situation remains extremely precarious. The Good Friday Agreement successfully brought an end to thirty years of conflict that claimed more than 3,500 lives. However, small, radical factions have continued to operate in the shadows, attempting to provoke a harsh response from British security forces or loyalist paramilitaries in the hopes of reigniting a broader cycle of violence.

PSNI Chief Constable Sir Hugh Orde urged calm and warned against knee-jerk security measures that could alienate nationalist communities. "This was a calculated attempt to drag us back to the past," Orde said. "The threat level from dissidents remains high, but the political and social landscape of Northern Ireland today is fundamentally different."

Across Belfast, ordinary citizens expressed anger and anxiety, with many fearing a return to the violence of their youth. Spontaneous peace vigils were organized in several towns on Tuesday, drawing people from both Catholic nationalist and Protestant unionist backgrounds. 

As security forces launch massive manhunts to track down the killers, the coming days will test whether Northern Ireland's political institutions, forged in the crucible of compromise eleven years ago, can withstand this direct assault from those determined to tear the peace apart.

"These people are intent on trying to drag us back to the past," McGuinness said. "I was a member of the IRA, but that war is over. The people who carried out this attack are attempting to undermine the political process."

While political analysts warn that the shooting represents the most serious challenge to Northern Ireland’s stability in a generation, the swift, united front presented by former bitter enemies has reaffirmed the strength of the peace institutions.
